scenes.narration: Why would thousands of people stand in the snow before dawn, in the capital of the Soviet Union, just to buy a hamburger?

On January thirty-first, nineteen ninety, people began lining up near Pushkin Square in Moscow as early as four in the morning. By the end of the day, thirty thousand customers had walked through the doors of the first McDonald's in the Soviet Union, a record for any opening day in the company's history. For a few years, that hamburger became a symbol of the Cold War coming to an end. Thirty-two years later, it became a symbol of something else.

scenes.narration: How do you open a burger restaurant in a country where private business is not allowed?

Very slowly. The idea started in the nineteen seventies, with the Canadian arm of McDonald's. Beginning in nineteen seventy-six, one of its executives made the first of dozens of trips to Moscow, to lobby the officials of the Communist Party. In the Soviet Union, the state owned the shops, the farms and the factories. A foreign company could not just rent a building and start selling.

scenes.narration: The door opened only when the rules changed. In the late nineteen eighties, under perestroika, the Soviet Union began to allow joint ventures with foreign companies. On April twenty-ninth, nineteen eighty-seven, McDonald's Canada signed one with the Moscow city government. But there was a catch. The city kept the controlling share, fifty-one percent. The foreign partner was limited to forty-nine.

Let me draw how that deal worked. On one side, the city of Moscow, with fifty-one percent. On the other, McDonald's Canada, with forty-nine. Between them, one company, which would own the restaurant. The city brought the land, the permits and the political cover. McDonald's brought the money, the recipes and the know-how. And neither could do it alone.
In the end, it took fourteen years of work, and an investment of fifty million dollars, before the first burger was sold. And a big part of that money did not go into the restaurant at all.

scenes.narration: Because there was a problem nobody could negotiate away. The country had no reliable supply of the food a burger chain needs.

keyframes.label: A problem nobody could negotiate away

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: What do you do when the country cannot supply your ingredients?

A hamburger chain depends on the same bun, the same beef and the same potato, every day, in huge quantities. In the Soviet planned economy, nobody could guarantee that. So McDonald's decided to build the supply chain itself.

In nineteen eighty-nine, work began on a giant food plant in Solntsevo, on the edge of Moscow. It covered about one hundred thousand square feet. According to CBC, it was built to turn out fourteen thousand buns an hour, and ten thousand patties an hour. The building opened in nineteen ninety, just in time for the restaurant.

scenes.narration: Even the potatoes had to be imported, as seeds. McDonald's brought in Russet Burbank seed potatoes, the variety used for its fries, and trained Soviet collective farmers in how to grow bigger harvests. A burger restaurant was teaching farming to a superpower.

Let me draw the chain. Here are the farms, with the imported potato seeds. The crop goes into the plant, which makes the buns, the patties and the fries. And from the plant, the food goes to the restaurant on Pushkin Square. Every link in the chain was built from scratch, before a single customer walked in.

scenes.narration: By the end of January nineteen ninety, the chain was ready. Now the question was whether anyone would come.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: How many people will queue in the snow for a taste of the West?

The answer was, thousands. On January thirty-first, the first people arrived around four in the morning, in the dark and the cold. By the time the doors opened, thousands of people were waiting in line. Inside, the restaurant had twenty-seven cash registers ready for them.

scenes.narration: The staff had expected to serve around ten thousand meals that day. They served thirty thousand. No McDonald's anywhere in the world had ever served so many customers on its first day.
Let me draw what opening day looked like. Here is the plan, ten thousand meals. And here is what actually happened. Thirty thousand. Three times the plan, from a single restaurant, in a single day.

And it was not cheap. According to CBC, a meal cost about half a day's average wages. One man outside told a reporter that they were being ripped off. Still, the crowds kept coming. For many people, it was not really about the food.
The restaurant's first manager put it best. Many people talk about perestroika, he said, but for them it is an abstraction. I can touch my perestroika. I can taste it. Big Mac is perestroika.

Even the country's leadership saw it that way. Mikhail Gorbachev later called the restaurant a breakthrough, one which showed that new economic relations between the Soviet Union and the rest of the world were possible. A hamburger had become a piece of foreign policy.

scenes.narration: Less than two years later, the Soviet Union itself was gone. The restaurant stayed.

keyframes.label: the USSR was gone. The restaurant stayed.

scenes.narration: What happens to a symbol when the country around it changes?

In the new Russia, McDonald's slowly took control. In February nineteen ninety-six, it bought most of the city's shares in the joint venture, raising its own stake from forty-nine percent to eighty percent. The company that had once needed permission to open a single restaurant now ran the business.

And it grew. By twenty twenty-two, McDonald's had more than eight hundred and fifty restaurants in Russia. It owned about eighty-four percent of them, and ran most of them itself, rather than through franchise owners. They employed sixty-two thousand people. Together with its restaurants in Ukraine, the business brought in about nine percent of the company's annual revenue, around two billion dollars. For a brand built on burgers and fries, Russia had become one of its big markets.

Let me draw how the business changed. In nineteen ninety, one restaurant, forty-nine percent owned, in a joint venture with the state. By twenty twenty-two, more than eight hundred and fifty restaurants, mostly owned and run by McDonald's itself. That is what made the next step so expensive.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Then, in February twenty twenty-two, Russia invaded Ukraine.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: What does it cost to walk away from thirty years of business?

On March eighth, twenty twenty-two, McDonald's announced that it was temporarily closing its restaurants in Russia. Two months later, on May sixteenth, it went further. After more than thirty years in the country, it said, it would leave Russia for good, and it expected to book a charge of about one point two to one point four billion dollars. Its chief executive wrote that the company could no longer keep the Arches shining there.

Three days later, McDonald's agreed to sell the whole business to Alexander Govor, a local businessman who had run twenty-five restaurants in Siberia as a McDonald's licensee. The deal kept the employees in their jobs for at least two years. The price was never made public.

Let me draw what leaving cost. Here is McDonald's, and here is the Russian business, more than eight hundred and fifty restaurants. An arrow to the new owner, for a price nobody disclosed. And an arrow back, to the company's books. A charge of one point three billion dollars, mostly to write off what it had invested in Russia.

scenes.narration: In its results, McDonald's booked a charge of one point two billion dollars in the second quarter of twenty twenty-two, and one point three billion dollars over the first half of the year, related to the sale of its business in Russia.

And then came the strangest part. On June twelfth, twenty twenty-two, the restaurants began to reopen under their new owner, starting with the very same building on Pushkin Square. Same address, and under the deal, the same staff. Only the name had changed. It was announced just a couple of hours before the doors opened. Vkusno and tochka. Roughly, tasty, and that's it.

So what does one hamburger restaurant teach us about the world economy? That a business is never only a business. In nineteen ninety, a burger in Moscow meant the walls between East and West were coming down. It took fourteen years of politics to open the door, and one war to close it. The kitchens are still there, and so are the customers. What left was the name, and the idea that trade alone would keep the world together.
